name: Self-improvement 'glow-up' content

lead: Glow-up content is the genre of before-and-after videos and posts showing someone's changed appearance, often crediting skincare, fitness, grooming, clothing or procedures. Viewers use them as examples of what is possible and as templates for their own changes.

The chain is seeing the before-and-after, learning the methods credited, then copying changes to your own looks. It is a social-media descendant of the makeover genre, which has long featured in daytime talk shows, personal makeover television series and film. Few published sources study social-media transformation content specifically.

paras: People watch or save transformation posts, note the haircut, skincare routine, clothing or training approach credited, and try them. Many also post their own progress photos to track and share changes over time.

Before-and-after posts are selected and edited, so lighting, angles and timing can account for part of the difference. Related research links social-media exposure to appearance comparison, so some people find the genre motivating and others find it discouraging.

Glow ups: the internet's obsession with dramatic physical changes

angle.text: Transformation videos and posts show before-and-after changes in clothing, haircuts, skin, fitness or procedures, and viewers use them as templates and motivation for their own changes. The genre is popular; few studies examine it.

lead: Self-improvement 'glow-up' content refers to transformation videos and posts that present a before-and-after change in appearance, usually with the methods credited, such as skincare, grooming, fitness, style changes or cosmetic procedures. Viewers use it as a source of ideas and examples for their own appearance goals, and creators use it to document and share progress. It is a social-media descendant of the makeover genre, which Wikipedia describes as a radical change in appearance involving clothing, haircuts, cosmetics and sometimes weight loss, plastic surgery or dental work [1].

'Glow up' is a play on 'grow up'. Dictionary.com credits rapper Chief Keef with popularising it through his 2013 song 'Gotta Glo Up One Day' [2]. On TikTok the #GlowUp hashtag has been reported at tens of billions of views, with before-and-after compilations dominating it [3][4].

Researchers have studied how before-and-after images on Instagram and TikTok influence people considering cosmetic treatment, with reviews describing educational benefits alongside concerns about unrealistic expectations [5][6].

paras: Makeover television formats listed on Wikipedia include Queer Eye, What Not to Wear, Extreme Makeover and Pimp My Ride, and makeover plots recur in films such as My Fair Lady, Clueless, Mean Girls and The Devil Wears Prada.[1] Makeovers are usually viewed positively, as a way to start fresh or improve one's life.[1]

Wikipedia describes a film trope in which a character, usually a girl, undergoes a dramatic change in appearance or personality, with examples including Now, Voyager (1942), My Fair Lady (1964), Grease (1978), Clueless (1995), She's All That (1999), The Princess Diaries (2001), Mean Girls (2004) and The Devil Wears Prada (2006).[1]

The article also covers book and product spin-offs, including Suzanne Weyn's Makeover Series for teenage readers and Christopher Hopkins's 2008 book Staging Your Comeback on beauty for women over 45.[1]

Dictionary.com defines a glow-up as a positive personal transformation involving changes in appearance and style plus growth in confidence and maturity, and traces early social-media use of the phrase to November 2013 posts referencing Chief Keef; it entered mainstream coverage by 2020 and 2021, including a Newsweek piece on TikTok users pairing old yearbook photos with current ones [2].

A 2021 article on TikTok describes the #GlowUp hashtag as dominated by before-and-after compilations, with the trend growing during the pandemic [3]. A 2020 student-newspaper piece reported over 4 million Instagram results for #glowup and 14.7 billion TikTok views, and described '24-hour glow up' challenge videos [4]. Some creators, including LGBTQ+ and transgender people sharing medical-transition before-and-after content, describe such posts as validating [4].

Wikipedia describes virtual makeover software that lets users apply cosmetics, hairstyles and eyewear to a photo of a face to preview a look, with real-time versions now using phone camera tracking; named examples are Visage Technologies' MakeApp, L'Oreal's Makeup Genius and Oriflame's Makeup Wizard.[1] These tools sit alongside transformation posts as ways for people to preview or document a change in appearance.

Transformation posts commonly pair a before image with an after image and name the steps behind the change, such as a skincare routine, haircut, training block, wardrobe change or cosmetic procedure. Among 500 adults who had upper eyelid surgery, 64 percent named before-and-after images as the most influential social-media content [6]. Reviews of dental content describe both educational value and concern about unrealistic expectations [5].

Commentators argue that glow-up content can equate 'better' with weight loss or narrow beauty standards [3], that it presents the result as final and omits the long effort behind it, and that praise for weight loss can reinforce disordered eating thinking [4]. Others see it as positive personal growth [4].

A 2026 narrative review reports that Instagram and TikTok drive interest in whitening, veneers and orthodontics, finding educational benefits alongside unrealistic expectations and misleading before-and-after images.[5]

A 2026 cross-sectional study of 500 adults in Saudi Arabia having upper eyelid surgery found that 88 percent reported some social media influence and that before-and-after images were the most influential content, cited by 64 percent; strong influence was associated with slightly lower three-month satisfaction, mainly linked to recovery expectations.[6]

A 2026 scoping review of 58 studies reported that appearance-focused social media use is consistently linked to body dissatisfaction and body surveillance in adolescent girls and young women, and that body-positive and body-neutral content appeared most protective.[7] A 2026 randomised trial of 150 young women found that viewing fitspiration TikTok videos increased social comparison, appearance concerns and sadness compared with control content.[8] These studies concern appearance-focused content generally rather than transformation posts specifically.
No studies found on transformation content as a genre. Related research on social media, before-and-after images and body image is summarised in the sections above [5][6][7][8].
